The gameplay is very much the same from Asylum and the ability to play as Catwoman is a very welcome addition. Sadly, the riddler collectibles are much harder to collect now. Though not as great as Arkham Asylum, this is still one of the best Batman games ever made.

I'm playing the Arkham trilogy for the first time, in reverse. Some spoilers for both City and Knight. 


Things I loved: 
- The brutal, barren, claustrophobic design of City. 
- Some of the best combat in the series, although more primitive than its sequels. 
- City is much more grounded (literally and figuratively). 
- Diverse boss cast, and, for its time, the best boss fights in the series. 
- A game which strives to be more.

Minor Critiques/Insights: 
- I found the level design to be confusing. 
- Inclusion of unavoidable Catwoman storyline could be for better or worst. Her combat mechanics in City exceed that of Knight.
- No Robin outside of a cutscene in the main storyline. 
- Story seems to rely heavily on the previous game. 

The only thing really wrong with City is the passage of time and advancements in game technology. 

7/10. 
Overall: City lands in low S tier, with Knight lowered to a strong B.

This Batman game will always have a special place in my heart. This game feels like an absolute love letter to the fans. Especially with the various cameos, easter eggs, and dialogue references that comic readers can easily point out. The vibe of the setting matches the chaotic open world perfectly, from large fires to thugs littered throughout the streets the city always feels like it needs saving. The story is filled with twists and really awesome fights throughout the game, stealth is just like the other games in the trilogy and is always fun striking fear into your enemies. Combat easily reminds you that you're playing as Batman and it's totally badass. Enemy variations leave you constantly planning how to take everyone down during the heat of battle. Overall, this is one of my favorite games of all time and it still holds a candle to a lot of single player games today despite it's age. The devs really cooked with this one and you should defintely check it out if you find yourself looking for a really great single player game.

I wrote a little about this in my Asylum review, but if you're a casual fan looking where to start with the Arkham games, I feel like Arkham City is a great place. Fantastic story, more refined game-play, and good graphics that have aged well in 2025, and gives you necessary context for Knight. I'm looking forward to exploring Arkham City more and wrapping up some more side quests (though...I'm not looking forward to dealing with Riddler's trophies...)

Note: I did have some performance issues during the [spoiler]Clayface boss fight when he turned into a boulder and crashed into the walls[/spoiler] where my frames totally tanked, but other than that this game runs very well. This game didn’t just reignite my Batman obsession—it threw gasoline on it and lit it with Zsasz’s lighter. Arkham City is a gritty, noir-soaked playground where every alley whispers secrets and every rooftop begs for a grapple hook.
You want iconic villains? Sure, Joker and Two-Face are here. But real fans know the thrill of stumbling into a side mission with Deadshot, or hearing the creepy monologue from Hush. And yes—Calendar Man is in the basement, waiting for you on holidays like a festive serial killer. Pure Batman gold.
The combat is smoother than Catwoman’s sarcasm, the story twists harder than Mad Hatter’s tea party, and the atmosphere? Straight out of a detective comic dipped in shadow and angst.
If you know who Professor Strange is without Googling, this game was made for you.
If you’ve ever said “I wish Azrael had more screen time,” welcome home.
If you think Batman should brood more and punch harder—this is your cathedral.

As the sequel to Arkham Asylum, this game raises the stakes and draws us deeper into Batman’s world. This time, we explore Arkham City, a walled-off section of Gotham where Hugo Strange keeps the city’s most notorious criminals. A mix of new and returning classic villains stands in Batman’s way, each more dangerous than the last.

One of the standout moments for me is the boss fight with Mr. Freeze, which demands every bit of your gameplay skill. It’s tough, but it’s also one of the most rewarding encounters I’ve played. The Mad Hatter side quest is wonderfully surreal, while Zsasz’s detective-style missions are tense and engaging.

A huge highlight is being able to play as Catwoman. Her whip, pouncing attacks, and fluid acrobatics make combat feel fresh and exciting, offering a perfect contrast to Batman’s bulkier fighting style. Along the way, new enemy types push you to adapt and refine your strategies.

Not everything landed perfectly for me. The Riddler’s Challenges didn’t hold the same magic as in Asylum. The tighter, more contained environment in the first game made those puzzles more satisfying to track down. In the sprawl of a larger city, the thrill was harder to replicate.

As of writing, I’ve finished the main story and started Harley Quinn’s Revenge. I can already tell that Arkham City has greater replay value than its predecessor, thanks to its bigger map, hidden quests, and layered challenges.

This is an incredible sequel—one that shows how much care, dedication, and attention went into Batman’s world-building. It’s immersive, addictive in the best way, and proof that superhero games can combine action and storytelling at the highest level.

A good sequel to Asylum, Arkham City features much of the same general gameplay and combat styles, and much of the same main characters, with some valuable additions and variations on enemies. Levels can often feel unintuitive and restrictive, but it's a good enough play, especially if you like the IP.

Playtime: 14.3 hours (PC, controller, Steam Deck)

[b]Overall:  8/10[/b]

[u]Narrative: 8/10[/u] - Arkham City follows the aftermath of the fall of the expansive penitentiary and has Batman attempting to foil Joker's and Harley's destructive plans. As with Asylum and fitting with the theme of Batman in general, the story is simple, but silly, isolated and effective, and has a slightly more entertaining and engaging story than Asylum. The fast-paced narrative doesn't necessarily touch on anything deep but fits perfectly in the world of Batman and never felt stale. Harley Quinn's Revenge was a thematic, valuable addition to the story. With the main story, there doesn't seem to be an appropriate narrative resolution with regard to the scale of chaos in Arkham City, which made it feel a bit disjointed toward the end.

[u]Visuals: 9.5/10[/u] - An entirely new open world was crafted for this game and it looks great, even by today's standards. It's very well-built and looks great from almost anywhere, looking in any direction, especially with the inclusion of the background/sky box assets, which serve to make the already-large open world feel even larger. Batman has a very unique art style and it's executed quite well in this game (as in Asylum). The lighting effects and use of color in Arkham City are both done well and make the world feel almost cartoon-oriented, to the benefit of the game. Although the entirety of the open world is basically the same place (Arkham City), there is enough visual variation to make each part of the map feel distinct, and for indoor areas to not feel repetitive. Character models look great.

[u]Audio: 9/10[/u] - Rocksteady upped their game on the music/score since Asylum. The score is fantastic and never got repetitive. The voice acting, like the first game, is great and fits the style of the subject content. Combat sound effects are done well and also in a cartoon-ish sort-of way. Spatial audio was a bit lacking but nothing audio-related got repetitive in this game.

[u]Gameplay: 7/10[/u] - The gameplay in Arkham City is very similar to that of Asylum, sending you all over the open world to attempt to foil Joker's and Harley's plans, using numerous gadgets along the way to access different areas. Combat is much the same as in Asylum, with some minor changes and additions. The combat simple but fluid and fun and the player can be as creative as they want to with the gadgets during combat. Combat, character movement, and stealth are inventive enough, and game mechanics are introduced often enough, to not feel repetitive throughout the game. However, quite a few boss battles, and battles otherwise, are really just about figuring out what you're supposed to be doing whilst dying several times. What the player is supposed to do is often not self-explanatory and I often experienced the game telling what to do with text on screen. I think some better coordination with the level design team is in order to better align player expectations with what they are served in the game.

[u]Character Design: 8/10[/u] - Arkham City features Batman and Catwoman, and at times, Robin, as they try to stop Joker and Harley from destroying everything and killing everyone, with some special appearances by Clayface, Mr. Freeze, and others, which provides some nice variety through a playthrough without simply recycling enemies from the first game. The dialogue is simple but entertaining and effective and fits the theme of Batman well. I appreciated the opportunity to switch between characters/character models after beating the game. Characters are modeled well, look good in game, and fit nicely with the environment design. What they did with Joker throughout the game was cool and advanced the narrative in a meaningful way.

[u]Environment and Level Design: 6/10[/u] - One of my gripes from Asylum was that the interiors are easy to get lost in and it can be very difficult to find your way to an exit back to the open world. Indoor areas are maybe even a bit more confusing in City than in Asylum. I got lost several times and where the player is supposed to go is often unintuitive. In fact, a lot of what the player is supposed to be doing at any time is often unintuitive. The levels make it seem like there are many different ways to complete them, but they are often set up in a restrictive way which limits viable strategies immensely. There is also a lack of environmental storytelling as compared to Asylum. However, visually, all of the levels and world in general look great, and there is a great consistency and adherence to the art style.

[u]Personal Engagement: 8/10[/u]

[u]Personal Replay Value: 6.5/10[/u] - NG+

[u]Performance: 9/10[/u] - 2k144 on PC, no performance issues. Flawless performance on Steam Deck. Steam Cloud saves enabled. Minus one for the annoying title sequence on launch.

It takes everything that was great about Arkham Asylum and makes it bigger. This time you’re not stuck in one building—you get to explore a huge section of Gotham that’s been turned into an open-air prison. The freedom to glide around the city and drop down on criminals feels awesome and makes you feel even more like Batman.
The combat system is just as smooth as before, maybe even better, since there are more gadgets and moves to use. The predator sections are still there too, and the bigger environments give you more ways to be creative when taking out enemies.
The story is packed with Batman’s most famous villains. You’ll run into Penguin, Mr. Freeze, Two-Face, and of course the Joker. Some side missions even let you face off against characters like Deadshot and Riddler, which makes the world feel full of things to do beyond the main plot.
The city itself is dark, gritty, and fun to explore. Gliding across rooftops never gets old, and hunting down Riddler trophies can be pretty addictive. Just like the first game, the voice acting is top-notch—Mark Hamill’s Joker is especially memorable here.
Overall, Batman Arkham City is a bigger and better experience than Asylum. It gives you more freedom, more villains, and more reasons to keep playing. If you enjoyed the first game, this one is a must.

This is my favorite game in the series tied with Arkham Origins.

It feels like everything that was great about the first game was improved on and refined to perfection, and some of the rougher bits were rounded out.

The world is much bigger than the first game, and it's absolutely full of great missions, including both side missions AND main story missions. It feels like this game has just the right scale for an open world. Big enough to not get boring, but small enough to not feel daunting or overwhelming. Because of this, the game feels alive, and like you can find a completely unique interaction anywhere.

The character writing is at some of its best in the whole franchise. Some of the weird characterization bits from the previous game have been whittled down by a LOT! The stakes are much bigger than the previous game, and the characters, although they're still recognizable to their comic and animated counterparts, feel much more realistic and believable than the last game.

This game has some of the best art direction I've ever seen from this series. With notes of Tim Burton's influence, the architecture of the city feels exactly like how I'd picture my ideal version of Gotham City. I absolutely love the graphics in this game. The character designs are also FANTASTIC.

The story and gameplay is much more dynamic than the last game. The combat flows fantastically, and there's a learning curve that makes it really fun to keep on coming back to. You switch between playing as multiple characters throughout the game, which keeps things fresh.

Overall, I would say that this game is ABSOLUTELY worth playing and has nearly zero flaws whatsoever.

[i]Batman: Arkham City[/i] is an action-adventure game developed by Rocksteady Studios and published by Warner Bros. Interactive Entertainment.

[b]Story[/b]
I suggest playing through Arkham Asylum first, as events from that game are used as a setup to setting of this one.

Arkham City takes place 18 months after Arkham Asylum events. Taking credit for stopping Joker's siege, director Sharp becomes a Mayor of Gotham City. Declaring Asylum no longer suitable, he creates immense prison enclosure known as Arkham City inside Gotham's slums, taken care of by mysterious Hugo Strange while monitored by private military firm TYGER Security. Our protagonist, Bruce Wayne, opposes that idea and ends up in a titular prison himself. Here as Batman he wants to find out more about mysterious Protocol 10 and real intentions behind the prison.

[b]Gameplay[/b]
If you played Arkham Asylum, you already know what to expect as City builds up upon gameplay from previous game, providing third person open world venture where you will investigate, explore, stealth and brawl through the prison as our favourite Caped Crusader, searching for truth (and few faces to soak your fists in).
First thing you will experience is the main dish of the game- combat. Punch, kick, smack thugs before they smack you to avoid a dreadful fate of watching villians laugh in your face as you lose and reload a checkpoint. Counter or dodge incoming attacks, chain up combinations to gain speed and power, utilize plenty of gadgets to surprise your opponents. Game provides improved version of the "Freeflow" combat system, meaning you can now perform more moves, such as option to counter multiple attacks at once or being able to chain combinations for long enough to unleash deadly special attacks. Enemies can be armed with different armor and weapons, forcing you to adjust your moves accordingly.

Sometimes you get a chance to resolve encounters silently. Similar scenario as with first game, utilize vantage points, environment, detective vision and your gadgets to eliminate enemies without them noticing you. Watch as fear strikes their minds and heartpulse keeps rising with each performed takedown on their buddies, but just like in combat, thugs are a bit more Bat-proof this time so they come with more firearms, jammers and extra tools that will make your life harder, as tides can quickly shift back and forth. Know when to strike and when to wait for opportunity, or just create your own!

Arkham City opens up the area, providing way more space to explore. Glide, grapple and sprint around looking for collectibles that expand the narrative and lore, side activities, or just seek out local thugs waiting for a fight! (Or to be knocked out silently by a sneaky Bat.) Fans favourite Riddler returns with his trophies and riddles, while other villians make an appearance in side quests spread all over the prison, unlockable as you progress through the story. Same applies to gadgets, so you might have to wait a bit to obtain a tool or two before you can enter certain buildings or collect specific trophies. No pressure, you can always return to every area you visited.

Combat and exploration grant you experience points, earn enough to level Batman up and unlock new skills, moves, or improve gadgets.

[b]Playtime, other modes[/b]
It took me roughly 13 hours to complete everything in Arkham City. After beating the story you unlock New Game Plus where you can utilize everything you have unlocked with increased overall difficulty to balance it out. Additionally there is "Riddler's Revenge" mode, where you tackle on different challenge maps and campaigns for medals! Fair to say you can spend a bit more time in City than you might think at first glance, if interested. Especially as this version comes with extra DLC, Catwoman content, and extra characters in RR mode.

[b]Impressions[/b]
Out of the gate I will go out with a very bold claim- Arkham City is probably the best sequel I ever had a pleasure to play. A textbook definition of how they should be made. It's not a revolution, but an evolution. If you played Asylum you feel right at home almost instantly as game keeps same great controls and fantastic core gameplay allowing you to quickly get into action, increasing and opening up the location where game takes place, addition of side quests and expanded lore make it feel like an entirely new experience. Already great combat is now reaching superb levels, it's smooth, it's intuitive, with very tight controls and top notch precision when it comes to inputs as if game knows which thug you want to hit before you even do. Some annoying moments from Asylum where Batman in the middle of combination would decide to punch ghosts are gone, combined with new moves and gadgets it practically makes you beg for as many enemies on screen as possible to go wild.

But game knows when to slow down, when to give you a stealth section to showcase pretty solid enemy AI, allowing you to fully lean into Batman's strategic side with various gadgets, careful planning and utilization of environment to his advantage. Quite frankly it's a shame that because game is no longer as linear as first title, plus complete change of area where game takes place so it's almost impossible to just give you a stealth section in the middle of the city, it doesn't actually have that many of those section. But when you get them, it's an absolute treat to play.

Asylum no doubt had it's own unique atmosphere, but City is no slouch in that department either. Prison filled with crime in the middle of gang wars, with secrets on top of secrets, the mash of destroyed slums with iconic locations, freedom you get to explore it and encounter many more and lesser known villians across short yet satisfying side quests, it hits right. Fortunately game never feels too long, it doesn't drag on, even if you decide to dive into the madness that is collecting those forsaken trophies.
Fantastic audiovisual side, strong art direction, top of the game performance from voice actors and animators, game even today looks fairly impressive. Forgot to even mention expanded extra side mode of the game in which you can spend plenty hours, if running around Arkham City gets boring for you.

If there something...mixed, I can say about this game, it would probably be about the story. In my book the main villian in this one was a bit..disappointing? Especially as he was pretty much a "main face" when it came to promoting the game. I expected a better conclusion of certain arcs and felt like it could have focus on just one story, instead of jumping around and trying to have two main storylines branching out and at least for me, that never really worked. So yeah, story is enjoyable but I would like it to go into a different direction.

Nonetheless, Arkham City is simply superb. Easy recommendation. Combat feels great, explorating feels enjoyable, still holds up visually and it's a treat for fans of DC/Batman.

[b]Final words and conclusion[/b]
Said it before, gonna say it again, GOTY Edition comes with everything released so you get all the fun stuff- alternative costumes, post-main game DLC and extra characters- in one pack!

Batman: Arkham City improves pretty much everything from first game while still focusing on core strenghts- fantastic combat, great audiovisuals and intriguing exploration. Buy it, play it, enjoy it.

[h1]Batman: Arkham City Review[/h1]

[hr]
[h1]Overview[/h1]
Takes everything Arkham Asylum did right and turns the dial up. Smoother combat, slick traversal, bigger cast, tighter stealth, and a city that begs you to glide across it at 3 a.m. Easy recommendation.

[hr]
[h1]Setup & World[/h1]
Arkham City is a walled chunk of Gotham turned into a prison district under Hugo Strange. You drop in as Batman to unravel Protocol 10 while the rogues gallery turns the streets into turf wars. The map is not huge for the sake of it; it is dense, readable, and full of landmarks. It keeps Asylum’s eerie, lived-in mood but lets you stretch your wings.

[hr]
[h1]Traversal[/h1]
No web swinging needed. Grapnel boost into a glide, dive to build speed, pull up, repeat. It takes a little practice and then it clicks, and suddenly you are threading alleys and water towers like you own the skyline. Moving is half the fun.

[hr]
[h1]Combat & Stealth[/h1]
Freeflow feels sharper and faster. More enemy types, more gadgets, and more ways to keep your combo clean. Predator rooms add new tricks, letting you set traps, separate thugs, and disappear before anyone points a finger. It is everything you liked in Asylum with a smoother rhythm.

[hr]
[h1]Story & Villains[/h1]
You juggle Strange’s Protocol 10, Joker’s condition, Penguin’s power plays, Mr. Freeze’s unforgettable boss fight, and a late twist with Clayface. The pacing stays tight, and the Joker material lands hard. It keeps the surprises coming without wasting your time.

[hr]
[h1]Catwoman Content[/h1]
Short playable segments with her own move set, gadgets, and upgrades. Fun palette cleanser during the story, and you can free roam as her after. It makes the city feel like a shared stage, not just Batman’s playground.

[hr]
[h1]Riddles, Secrets, Challenges[/h1]
More than Asylum, with some gated by later gadgets or routes. Most puzzles reward map knowledge rather than checklist grinding. Challenge maps can feel repetitive if you chase every medal, but swapping between Batman, Catwoman, Robin, and Nightwing helps keep it fresh.

[hr]
[h1]Music & Atmosphere[/h1]
The score leans into brooding strings and punchy cues that rise right when you land a big combo or perch over a patrol. Radio chatter, Joker announcements, and wind off the rooftops sell the space. It is subtle enough to stay out of the way, strong enough to make gliding laps feel like a scene.

[hr]
[h1]Pacing & Length[/h1]
Just right. The main path never drags, side stories slot in naturally, and the city’s size keeps backtracking painless. Easy to finish the campaign and still feel excited to hunt secrets.

[hr]
[h1]Why It Works[/h1]
It expands in the places that matter. The world breathes, the combat sings, stealth setups let you play creatively, and traversal ties it all together. It feels like a sequel that actually learned and refined instead of just getting bigger.

[hr]
[h1]Verdict[/h1]
One of the best third-person action games around. If Asylum hooked you, City seals the deal. Play it, take a few victory laps over the skyline, and enjoy a Batman game that nails nearly every beat.

🦇 Batman: Arkham City Review 🦇

🕹 Length:
• 12–20 hours (main story + major side quests)
• 40+ hours for completionists
• +3–5 hours with DLC (Harley Quinn’s Revenge + Challenge Packs + Skins)

💰Price vs. Content: Excellent — a massive base game plus DLC that meaningfully expands replayability
 ⚙ Optimization: Strong overall, but still needs tweaks to unlock FPS (capped at 60 by default)
🎮 Difficulty: Fair on Normal; Hard, New Game+, and DLC challenges add serious difficulty

🎮 Gameplay

Batman: Arkham City takes everything Asylum started and evolves it into a sprawling, atmospheric open world filled with iconic villains, meaningful side activities, and some of the best combat/stealth gameplay ever designed.

The FreeFlow combat system is deeper, faster, and more tactical, with new enemy archetypes and expanded gadget integration. Predator (stealth) encounters are more open and creative, letting you plan takedowns in bigger, vertical environments.

Traversal is one of the game’s highlights: gliding across Arkham City with dive-bombs, grapples, and momentum chaining feels incredible — quick, stylish, and empowering.

Side missions enrich the world, each villain getting their own storyline (Mr. Freeze, Deadshot, Zsasz, Hush, and many more), while Riddler puzzles return with greater creativity and scale.

Challenge Mode is expanded with new maps, modifiers, and playable characters, making it a major part of the experience, especially for players who want mastery.

🧩 DLC Content Breakdown

🎭 Harley Quinn’s Revenge (Story DLC)

A short but story-heavy epilogue taking place after the main game.
• Play as both Batman and Robin
• New environments and enemy setups
• Darker tone with Harley leading her own gang
• Adds closure to certain story beats

Length: ~1.5–2 hours — short, but polished and atmospheric

🎮 Challenge Maps DLC

Includes multiple packs:
• Nightwing Bundle Pack
• Robin Bundle Pack
• Challenge Map Pack

Adds:
✔ New characters (Robin & Nightwing)
✔ Dozens of Combat and Predator challenges
✔ Extra achievements and progression paths
✔ Extremely replayable content for mastery-focused players

🦇 Skin Packs

Multiple Batman suits, including:
• Batman Beyond
• The Dark Knight Returns
• Year One
• Animated Series
• Sinestro Corps Batman

Purely cosmetic but beloved — adds flavor for replays and Showcase runs.

✅ The Good:
✔ Enormous open world full of atmosphere and secrets
✔ Best combat/stealth hybrid gameplay of its generation
✔ Superb story with memorable villains
✔ Challenge Mode + DLC adds dozens of extra hours
✔ Traversal is fluid, fast, and fun
✔ Harley Quinn’s Revenge gives meaningful post-game story content
✔ Character DLC (Robin & Nightwing) expands gameplay variety

❌ The Bad:
✖ FPS is locked at 60 unless manually edited — disappointing for modern systems
✖ Harley Quinn’s Revenge is short for a story DLC
✖ Some challenge maps can feel repetitive if you're not into mastery play
✖ Side missions can be easy to miss if you don't explore thoroughly

💻 Technical Aspects

🎨 Graphics: Stylish, atmospheric, and surprisingly detailed for its age
🎶 Sound: Legendary voice acting (Conroy, Hamill, North) and a powerful orchestral score
🐞 Bugs: Mostly minor; some movement stutter until the FPS cap is manually removed

⭐ Final Verdict

Batman: Arkham City remains one of the greatest superhero games ever created. Its combination of world-building, combat depth, emotional storytelling, and replay value is unmatched. With DLC included — especially the challenge packs and Harley Quinn’s Revenge — it becomes an even more complete experience for fans of Batman and action games.

👉 Rating (Complete Edition): 10/10

Text Review:

Pros:
-Good visuals with a lovely darkness (Graphics still hold up, if they have aged, have grungy elements and the open world can feel empty sometimes with preference of rooftop travel and big flooded sections. The archtypical hero/ villain design isn't for everyone - hyper masculine walls of meat and women with their sex appeal. The combat animations are seamless!)
-Good, familiar, orchestral, superhero music (Good enough that it doesn't feel cliche. Lovely and adds to the darkness of the city and ramps up for tension during stealth segments as you take guards out to mirror how dire their situation is)
-Great voice acting, if mostly because of Mark Hamil as "The Joker" (The thug small talk can be intrusive if you don't want to miss dialogue and have to stop and listen and sometimes it is repetitive but it's extensive in their stereotypical goon glory. Batman can be inhumanly emotionless and the super villians quite theatrical, sometimes this works, sometimes it doesn't)
Fun, supremely refined combat (The familiar Assassin's Creed/ Arkham system of attack, counter, gadget but this franchise is one of the pioneers of the system and arguably did it the best. Not that hard, even on hard, but it's tense, requires focus and rewards mastery and move variety with more experience points - If you can remember all the different gadgets and moves) 
Good, fun stealth system (It's fun to terrify hench people)
-Fun traversal of Arkham city (It can get a bit repetitive though, grapple on roof, reel in, launch, glide, repeat until at your destination, sometimes from one end of the map to the other AROUND Wonder Tower)
-Fun collectathon (Riddler trophies to collect through puzzles and traversal, riddles that require you take a picture of a certain feature. They're usually a mild challenge, if that, but a nice change from punching etc. However there are so many of them!)
-Good amount of content (Has score chase challeges outside of the campaign too for inbetween game fun)

Maybes:
-Sometimes the boss fights involve stealth and standard brawling instead of going up against a massive beast but the music and cinematics make sure it's still as epic and I personally like this variety it's just some will consider this approach a bit anti-climacrtic
-Overall plot and dialogue is OK (Some thug small talk is forced to sound macho and not PC). Has a surprisingly touching moment and twist but one of the other twists was ultimately predictable (Who else could it have been really?) and "Protocol 10" is a very dry super villain plot especially after all the convoluted problem solving and story you had to wade through to unveil it (It was far less clever than we were lead to believe). The in depth lore in the codex is still great though.

Cons:
-Has some unrefinements (Body physics for downed enemies are loose and that is made very visible during slow motion, cinematic close-ups for finishing strikes,some graphical issues maybe, and unless I am mistaken for me the "Identity Thief Killer" quest line had trouble triggering but I don't think it's the most common issue and eventually it worked. Nothing serious really)

The game’s mechanics and gadgets were excellent — none of the tools felt unnecessary or out of place. Everything had a clear purpose, and they made the gameplay and combat feel dynamic rather than stiff or repetitive. The combat speed was perfectly balanced too — not so slow that it became boring, and not so fast that it felt confusing.

As for the game’s atmosphere, it was truly captivating. The dark and gloomy tone of Gotham was portrayed perfectly, and the characters fit right into that world — it genuinely felt like you were dealing with real maniacs.
.
.
The only downside was the handling of side mission boss fights. They didn’t get enough attention, and most of those fights felt underwhelming despite the effort needed to reach them. For example, the Riddler boss fight — after collecting tons of trophies and solving countless puzzles, it all ends in a simple room with an easy takedown. It was a bit disappointing, especially since Riddler had been part of the story from the very beginning.
In the end, though, I definitely recommend this game — it’s absolutely worth playing more than once. Each time you replay it, you’ll notice new details you might’ve missed before.

Batman: Arkham City delivers everything you want from stepping into the cowl and then some. From the first glide over Gotham’s icy rooftops, you feel the precision, power, and menace of the Dark Knight.

Combat is a fluid ballet of strikes, counters, and gadget tricks, rewarding timing and creativity so every fight feels sharp and cinematic. Stealth is equally satisfying, as you drop silently from gargoyles or use smoke to vanish is pure predator fantasy.

Gotham itself is the star: a sprawling, atmospheric playground of neon grime and lurking villains. Side missions weave naturally into the main story, making the city feel alive with danger and mystery. Kevin Conroy and Mark Hamill deliver career-best performances, giving every cutscene the weight of a classic graphic novel.

The Game of the Year edition packs in all the DLC and still looks striking years later, proof that strong design outlasts hardware cycles. Tight, stylish, and endlessly replayable, Arkham City remains the definitive Batman experience and the benchmark for every superhero game that followed.

During the installation process, along with the DirectX libraries, another program will be installed called AMD Dual-Core Optimizer which was meant to improve the performance on systems that run Windows XP and use old AMD Dual-Core CPUs.

On PCs that run Windows Vista and later and/or an Intel CPU, you won't need that program because it will impact the performance and cause other issues.

Unfortunately when you launch the game for the first time you don't get the choice to decline the installation of AMD Dual-Core Optimizer (that's why I left a negative review).
In order to stop that program from being installed, do as follows:

If the program is already installed, you should uninstall it. Go to "Programs and Features", select "AMD Dual-Core Optimizer" and click "Uninstall" (perhaps it will take a while, do not cancel the process and wait); afterwords, reboot the PC.

1) Go to the installation folder of the game (right click on the game title -> properties -> local files tab -> browse local files)
2) Open "installscript.vdf" (right click -> open with -> use Notepad)
3) Scroll down until you see the word "AMD", followed by a bunch of code between the two perpendicular { and } brackets; delete that portion of code, beginning from the word "AMD" to the last perpendicular bracket (note that you must leave the brackets on the left side and everything else)
4) Save the file. Make sure you didn't delete anything that has to do with DXSetup, VCRedist_x86 and DotNetFx35
5) When you're done, go to the "Setup" folder and delete "amd_dc_opt.exe" (this is an optional step, just to be safe)

If you've done everything correctly, when you launch the game the installation of AMD Dual-Core Optimizer won't start.

REMEMBER TO NOT VERIFY THE INTEGRITY OF GAME FILES, OTHERWISE YOU MUST REPEAT THE PROCEDURE

"Batman: Arkham City? More like Batman: Arkham Pity. This sequel to the overrated Arkham Asylum fails to deliver anything remotely worthy of the Dark Knight's legacy.

Let's start with the gameplay—or lack thereof. Sure, you get to glide around Gotham City as Batman, but what's the point when the combat feels like you're just mashing buttons with no real skill or strategy involved? It's repetitive, shallow, and about as satisfying as punching a pillow.

And don't even get me started on the story. You'd think that throwing Batman into a sprawling open-world environment filled with iconic villains would lead to some epic storytelling, but instead, you're treated to a convoluted mess of a plot that's more interested in shoehorning in as many fan-favorite characters as possible than actually telling a coherent narrative.

But perhaps the biggest sin of all is the game's complete lack of innovation. It's basically just Arkham Asylum with a fresh coat of paint and a bigger sandbox to play in. There's nothing here that hasn't been done better in other open-world games, and it's clear that the developers were content to coast on the success of the first game rather than take any risks.

And let's not forget about the technical issues. Glitches, bugs, and performance problems abound, making it feel like the game was rushed out the door before it was ready for prime time.

In the end, Batman: Arkham City is a forgettable sequel that adds nothing of value to the series. Save yourself the disappointment and stick to the comics."

Gameplay :

The stealth sections are way too easy, enemy being really dumb with extremely exploitable vantage point/grate takedown, alongside the extremely overpowered Detective vision just made it a matter of patience with barely any thinking required, since you can just hide easily because of their AI, there is usually no risk in getting caught cause you can just go inside a grate or repeteadly jump between vantage points, and rinse and repeat. 

The combat is really good and I played the entire game in hard difficulty, however the severe lack of enemy types just means that 3 hours into the game you've experienced the entire gameplay. There's the one armed thug, which I have no idea if they're supposed to make it harder, I mean, the only thing missing is for them to tell you when to dodge because you can't block it. Then the swinging "titan" which requires another different input to fight. Then the ones with the blade, which requires another different input to fight. Now these sounds good, but they were never really utilized in a way where they all perfectly work together to challenge the peak of the player's skill. I don't think they were willing to fully commit, which for me, really hurt the potential of the combat and almost made the game unbearably boring to finish. It was fun for sure, but after a while I stopped caring because I couldn't get engaged when the game barely throws anything my way that will require more than three brain cells to do.

The bossfights were decent if not bad, the entire point of the combat is a 360 degree combat, with emphasis on awareness. The bossfights being some sort of cuphead projectile dodging game was way too outside what the gameplay is about that it felt jarring, this isn't Dark Souls where'd you spam roll to dodge, doing that in the Clayface and R'as al ghul fight was just too awkward. However, the bit in the bossfights where you'd have to dodge Clayface while fighting off multiple small clayface was good. Because you know, it challenges the skill you've been honing during the game. Uniqueness and variety is good, but doing it for the sake of just doing something differently even thought the entire core of your game does not support it is not. This is the equivalent of platforming with suddenly breaking floor and dying instantly as Bed Of Chaos in a game about learning your enemies' moveset, dodging and counterattacking which is Dark Souls.  The Mister Freeze fight was tedious, you only need to take him down twice, to know all that you need to do. Doing it 8 more times was boring. He's extremely smart and dumb at the same time, adapting so that a trick will not work twice, but not learning to change his approach. 


And there's the hacking part, if you can call that gameplay. They exist to slow down the game, they're not engaging in any way. A few of them is fine, but they are way too prevalent in the entire game. 


STORY 

Story is decent, held down at being good because of Hugo,  I just couldn't get myself invested with the whole Hugo Thing, how he speak is just so annoying, he has zero charisma, and he speak so "smart" but doesn't sound threatening, he's so one dimensional in his dialogues and delivery that it was painful. The Joker part was better, his lines were good, delivery was good and when he talks you want to listen. It's because of his attitude, how he acts and carries himself, which if you put Hugo Strange in there, is a statute when it comes to being alive so I have no idea why he was even there. The twist was eh. There's another one, great. Totally didn't see that one coming because of the Joker looking deathly sick and healthy as a horse in another scene. Let's be honest, There being two doesn't matter. In detective stories, twists are good, because throughout the story, you're not just given clues, but you are also given misdirection. So when the reveal happens, you think yourself an idiot, not because there's a twin brother that you didn't catch up on, but because you suspected his sister. In Arkham City, the twist is just that there's a twin brother. Even if you pick upped on the clues, the only question you ask is "Wait, is there a different Joker or something?" You don't ask yourself the why. because there is no why, he just did it. That could be the real Joker holding down Talia, but instead of all that stuff, he just shoot her down instantly. Which would result in the same thing, no twin twist needed. 

Overall, I'd give it a 6/10. With the Joker and the combat being the sole good parts of the game

God fucking dammit Steam needs a "mixed" review.

If there is anyone out there who still doesn't own it, I would actually recommend this game to people who like:
- Batman lore
- open-world games
- streamlined reaction time based combat mechanics

My problem is that I like neither.

There are some things that this game does *very* well. Moving around the city by gliding and jumping from roof to roof, listening to the bad guys chatter, swooping in and fighting crime, and the whole being Batman thing feels really good. Graphics-wise it is still pretty impressive. The story is interesting (it depends on how much you like the lore I guess). The production value (world design, voices and dialogue) is insane for a 6 year old game. 

I just don't think it's deserving of that 95% rating and those remarks of it being "one of the best games ever" that people keep throwing around. It's actually a simple and linear game, cleverly disguised as an open-world game and with a very well executed Batman skin on top. None of the game mechanics are intrinsically "fun" or valuable on their own. They only make sense once you put the Batman skin on top of them and most of them are fluff, to keep you busy or advance the story line. Combat is basically a very elaborate cut scene, whose outcome is decided through quick time events (see the on-screen prompt, react by pressing the proper button). The combat system is what dissapointed me the most I'd say. "Detective mode" is basically 3D pixel hunting. Stealth is mediocre, feels tacked on and scripted. The "open world" part is just there to keep you busy going from A to B while following the story.  The combat mechanics, gadgets, puzzles are all just thrown at you from the start and will create the illusion of a complex game, but a lot of it is just fluff. There really aren't a lot of mechanics to "master" in the game.

However, everything looks *cool as fuck* and I think that's where the game shines - if you aren't looking for particularly deep mechanics or a sense of challenge, the game is gorgeous and spectacular and is maybe enough to keep you glued. There's a lot of stuff "to do" and achievements to hunt so if that's your thing, you're going to love it. 

But if you're looking for something more interesting, deeper mechanics, more complexity layers, look elsewhere. This is definetly not a stealth game - it's no Thief, Hitman, Splinter Cell, Dishonored. It's a linear experience cleverly disguised as an open world game. And it's definetly not one of the best games ever. One of the best produced games ever, yes, but mechanics wise it's very shallow.

I finally played this game in 2022. I was a huge fan of Arkham Asylum, so naturally I bought Arkham City on sale. However, it was a transitional phase in my life, and I mostly went on hiatus from PC gaming, so this sat in my backlog. I'm now trying to clear some games out, and this was one of my top picks. How does it hold up all these years later, with rose-tinted memory of its predecessor?

One negative was just how unfocused and chaotic the story progression is. From the opening moments of the game, the story just barfs characters, flashbacks, lore, exposition, and comic book references, yet none of it feels in service to a greater narrative. It's the video game equivalent of celebrity name-dropping. They clearly tried to cover more of the Batman universe, but they've stretched themselves a bit too thin. I remember Asylum having a surprisingly compelling story with excellent progression, but this doesn't feel that way at all.

The game play is a similar story. It's structured like an open-world game, albeit with a relatively small open world. Throughout it are countless training missions, events, secrets, side missions, characters, collectibles, etc. If you've ever played one of those F2P mobile MMOs that just throws a bunch of stuff at the wall to see what sticks, that's what this feels like. Much like with those F2P games, I honestly think this game throws too much at you all at once. Ironically, if there's anything it gives the player gradually over time, it's the tools necessary to do everything. Hours into this game, I'm still unlocking new abilities needed to complete many of the challenges, which may sound like a good thing, but the game does a poor job of guiding the player through the progression. There are rarely ever tutorials, and when there are, they're almost never any good. There are also minimal indications of when something isn't yet accessible with the current set of abilities.

The level-up menus are so unhelpful that I never really know how to use the abilities I'm unlocking. Many of them are so situational that I just find myself pressing keys when prompts appear without having the time to read or understand them. In Asylum, it felt meaningful to unlock a new ability, and I generally understood the immediate impact it had on my ability to manipulate the game world.

I also think they did themselves a bit of a disservice when placing the main story missions in the open world. In fact, "open world" is maybe a bit misleading, because at least early in the game, there's a huge restricted zone up through the middle of the map, so it's basically a big upside-down U shape. This wouldn't be so bad if the story progressed linearly around the U before opening up the restricted zone for the late game, but the main missions seem to flip-flop between opposite ends of the map, so you're constantly having to traverse the entire perimeter, which ends up feeling like a chore. As if the designers couldn't help themselves, they even exacerbated this issue by introducing all kinds of silly ideas that conflict with this map layout. A perfect example is when you need to locate Mr. Freeze by monitoring temperature and following it to the coldest zone in the map. This sounds like a cool idea, except that the temperatures might lead you to the border of the restricted zone, and the place you get to might be all the way on the other side.

That being said, is this a bad game? Absolutely not. A lot of this inconsistency seems to stem from the fact that it's arguably one of the most ambitious games ever made. The fact that they stuffed so many little twists on what are effectively just prompts and quest triggers is technically impressive, and some of them do feel better than others. One that stood out for me was when interrogating Riddler's thugs. As part of a Riddler quest, you need to walk around, find groups of thugs, and take them all out except for a single designated informant, at which point Batman can lift them up by their throat and interrogate them. This serves 2 purposes: 1) show Riddler secret locations on the map; 2) when you've successfully collected enough Riddler secrets (which are themselves puzzles rather than just basic collectables), interrogating an informant will reveal the location of another hostage that will progress the Riddler story line. These functions should sound completely familiar to veteran gamers, but done in a unique way that integrates puzzles, secrets, and missions together, making all of them more compelling. Lots of the negative things I pointed out above are byproducts of the developer's efforts to go above and beyond in making compelling versions of common game tropes.

This last point is not so much positive or negative as it is subjective. I remember in the mid 2000s, there was this prevailing design trend of games becoming more forgiving and hand-holding, exemplified by games like Call of Duty: Modern Warfare which popularized regenerating health. Only a handful of exceptions like the Souls series were praised for embracing traditional design. Thankfully, this dichotomy is much more nuanced in today's game design, with plenty of acceptance for games throughout the spectrum. This game may not have come across this way when it came out, but playing it in 2022, this game definitely has elements of the Souls school of design, in that many of the challenges and puzzles are quite difficult and opaque. This actually stands in stark contrast to the main missions, as well as the first game in the series, which was known for being a very straightforward and elegant brawler that was accessible to players of all skill levels. You can absolutely breeze through the main story missions in this game and ignore the optional challenges, but if you do attempt them, there are numerous challenges that expect you to master the very fine nuances of the physics system and gadgets. Personally, I don't love this. It's not so much the difficulty level that bothers me, but rather that the challenge prompts do a poor job of clarifying what players need to do. A good example is when the game teaches you to press the Ctrl key to dive while gliding, but fails to mention that letting go of Ctrl puts you back into a horizontal glide. I spent hours trying to complete stupid physics challenges that seemed impossible, until I searched for completion videos on YouTube and discovered that you can do crazy things like dive down and then pull up into a tight space like a tunnel or doorway, which is obviously very useful. I suspect many, if not most, players will breeze through much of the game not knowing that such advanced techniques are possible. However, for the right kind of player, having to discover these things through repeated tries and experimentation might be half the fun, so I think it was worth mentioning as a more neutral point.

To close out, I think this game has not aged as well as its predecessor. One of my favorite games is God of War 2018, and in many ways, Arkham Asylum felt like a precursor to that game. It was a very streamlined, approachable, exciting brawler with compelling narrative and just enough hints of open world design to make the experience more compelling than most linear story-driven games. In contrast, Arkham City almost feels like Arkham Asylum and Genshin Impact had a baby. Many of the core mechanics that worked so well in Arkham Asylum are present here, but the developer's attempt to make an extremely varied open-world experience with every Batman reference imaginable comes at the expense of focus. I spent hours coming to grips with the basics of this game, and now that I feel like I finally get it, I'm not as hooked on it as I was with Asylum back in the day. If you're looking to try this series in 2022, I would recommend starting with Asylum before deciding if you want more. Arkham City is different enough that it doesn't replace the former, and I think the former does what it does better.

This game has similar problems to Prototype (2009). They give you an expansive-but-samey open world, with an overabundance of overpowered weapons, tools and abilities - and then the level designers have to restrict all that freedom to be able to tell any story - by corralling you into industrial facilities with only one route through them.

Early on, the fights with gangs of thugs felt surprisingly true to the 1960s TV series Batman, but for there to be any challenge they had to add thugs with guns, to turn each room into a puzzle. The whole gangs aspect of Batman is aging badly - groups of identi-kit bodybuilders, standing in alleyways all day, even though there isn't anyone else around for them to rob. During the first several hours I ran in and mashed buttons rather than using the awkward controls to do anything else. The situational tactics stuff had a very slow learning curve, perhaps it gets more interesting but I doubted it would ever compare to Crusader: No Regret or a hundred others. Whatever the situation, Batman has too many options to choose from.

The storyworld/setting is so contrived that whatever the writers did with it was going to be boring, the plot unfolds in a linear fashion, using rubbish plot devices to set you up for the next twist. In the first few hours, Batman gets knocked out and tied up three times: by Dr Strange, then the Penguin, then the Joker. Like it's the only way the writers knew to advance from one chapter to the next. The individual cutscenes and lines of dialogue aren't any better - thugs give away clues whilst talking to each other every 5 minutes, Catwoman and Harley Quinn both make the same risque quips, and Batman betrays slight hints of inner fury... by saying... less... words.

I wish DC Comics and Hollywood and the people who make big-budget games would stop churning out paler and less demanding versions of Frank Miller Batman from 30 years ago, and that they would put some production cash into some of the niche Batmans. We don't again need to see what a kids' pantomime would look like if they spent millions of dollars on it.

*SIGH* Another potentially good game, completely killed by horrible development designs. This game is a huge let down for me. Not because it's a complete pile of rubbish, but because what it does well, it does incredibly well.

COMBAT. Combat in this game is probably the most satisfying hand to hand combat that I've ever experienced. You feel like you are in an action movie, the movement is smooth and intuitive. But fighting against opponents with guns is a real fun killer. You have the batclaw, which can be upgraded to disarm the gunmen that you experience. However, even after upgrading it to do so, you still can't disarm the gunmen until the third or fourth attempt. By that time, it's already too late. The reason being is that you never fight one opponent with a gun. It's either all people with melee weapons (FUN) or all gunmen (NOT FUN), which will mow you down extremely quickly. If the batclaw actually worked then it wouldn't be a problem and you could overcome this obstacle with skill. You are totally Batman in a movie, except when it comes to gunmen. The bat boomerang or even a claw being shot at the gun of an opponent isn't enough to disarm them. Even beating them to a pulp won't cause them to drop their guns. *SMH*

PHONE CALLS: There are side missions given to you by phone from ringing payphones. You have a certain amount of time to get to the next payphone and answer it, otherwise you fail. The problem is that most of the phones are guarded by several enemies who will fight you and not allow you to answer the phone. If you play perfectly, and get to the phone, you will have about 15 seconds at most to answer the phone. This isn't a problem if you are psychic and know ahead of time where the phone call will send you to answer the next phone. You just clear out the enemies ahead of time and then answer the phone that you are being sent to. But if you lack clairvoyance, you can't possibly take out the enemies and answer the phone in time. Seriously, who thought that this was a good idea?

RIDDLER MISSIONS. The real riddle is actually finding where to go for the mission. You will see a marker on your mini map telling you where to go, you head there, and there is nothing visible. You use your detective vision, which has every high tech gadget that you can think of,. Predator vision, plus every kind of gadget from a James Bond movie. This thing helps you see EVERYTHING through out the game. But not on the Riddler missions. Nope. Even when you have a paper thin wall, you can't see it. This makes absolutely no sense at all because seeing destructible walls is literally one of the powers you gain from using detective vision. Smooth brain 500 IQ decision there.

Finally the pacing of this game is just killed by needless obfuscation of what you are supposed to be doing. You can have your progress blocked in an area by trying to figure out how to get from point A to B. That's fine. I don't mind having to solve a puzzle. I get it that this game isn't a mindless beat em up game. Cool. But when you scan every room with your detective ability and can't see what you are supposed to do to shut down a steam valve, or have to watch a Youtube video to realize that you needed to slide under a door that's got a 3 inch gap between it and the ground all of the fun just turns to frustration. Make a slide under the door gap look....actually....possible so that a player would naturally think to try that. 

Only a few hours into the game, I've been to Youtube 3 times to figure out WTF I'm supposed to be doing. Instead of feeling like Batman in a Batman movie thinking: "What would Batman do?" I feel like I'm a rat, trapped in some game devs maze thinking: "What obscure corner did this dev hid a button behind that makes no sense at all?" This is why modern games suck. There is an amazing game here. The feel of Arkham city, the voice acting, the combat. It's all right there to be grabbed and ran with. To be enjoyed and leave you feeling satisfied...only to be plucked from your grasp by some stupid road block so that a game dev can turn a 15 hour gaming experience into a 20 hour gaming experience while you bash your head against the wall thinking: "How did it come to this? It's not rocket surgery. Just let my abilities work. Just let puzzles make sense!"

A reasonably 'okay' sequel to Asylum, Arkham City will satisfy any gamer eagerly looking to jump back into the Batman universe. Where the game falls short, it falls short hard. And where the game excels, it does so only teasingly. 

To be quick, the game throws in bosses so meaninglessly that you're often wondering if they're just doing it to increase the amount of hours it will take to beat the title. Sure, there are some cool fights. Batman's fight scene against Ra's al Ghul is probably one of the coolest single-player boss fights I've ever played. It's not predictable enough to be repetitive, and it's not unpredictable enough to be confusing. It's a visually gorgeous experience and shows just how well Rocksteady knows the engine they're working with. But this one fight is the only unique fight in the game, and is not the norm you'd want or expect from what is considered the best Batman video game series made.

The gameplay is what you'd expect if you played Asylum. It's the fluidity of the punch/kick combos when facing off against mobs of henchmen that has always made Rocksteady's franchise a lot of fun. But in City, Rocksteady has milked that way too much. Overcoming the odds of taking down five henchmen at once was cool. Doing it to a courtyard of thirty just becomes monotonous. And no, that doesn't happen just once in this game. It happens frequently.

I think it's the plot which is the most dissatisfying. There is no sense of attachment to Batman whatsoever. He is emotionally stoic and his dialogue is weak. He's desperate to be friends with all the villains and Rocksteady has tried hard to make it seem like the villains are just frail people who, with enough small talk, will eventually go out to coffee every morning with Batman. It's a weird dynamic and it's just simply not enjoyable. Joker, the primary plot-driving menace, is not enough of a focal point to carry you through the mounds of dullness the other villains throw at Batman.

Eh, I could say much more, but I don't want to take the time here. If you're interested in playing as Batman again in the world Rocksteady created, you'll find more of the same as what you saw in Asylum. There's a ton of nostalgic elements in this one, and while some of it is fun to play through, much of it is boring.

The original "Batman Arkham Asylum" remains one of the most enjoyable superhero games I've ever played. Sadly, I found this one to be a mixed experience. While it has some truly fun, memorable and immersive aspects, it also carries some truly irritating design decisions which keep the game from being something I can recommend.

Others have mentioned in reviewing the game that its new "open world" aspect sacrifices the tight, effective storyline which characterized the first game. This is absolutely true, in my opinion. The freedom is a shallow freedom, and it doesn't compensate for the sense of a fuller story lost.

But the biggest problem I had with Arkham City were the old-school boss fights -- super-tough enemies which typically have a "trick" to beating them which you must discover, typically by dying 20 -40 times in a row before you say "screw this" and go to YouTube looking for a walkthrough video.

Many of these boss fights I could suss out myself, but they were a chore; they were annoying; and ultimately, they were boring.

Worse, they were gameplay stoppers.

I stopped playing Arkham City for something like four (?)  months. Simply because of a contrived, brutal boss fight which needed to be completed before the game would progress. I knew I could beat it, eventually, but the prospect of grinding through it felt like work instead of play -- so I went and played other games instead.

The irony is, of course, that this Batman series has some of the best, most fluid and intuitive, hand-to-hand combat I've seen in gaming (provided you're playing with a game controller, and not a mouse and keyboard), but the old-school "survival grind" boss fights constantly devalue this innovation. Batman goes from being an awesome fighter to a repeated casualty semi-regularly.

Ultimately, I can't recommend Batman: Arkham City. For me, the irritation outweighed the innovation, and the gain of the open-world didn't compensate us for the loss of a focused first-rate Batman story, as in the original. The plot here is good, but there isn't enough of it, in my opinion.

If you've gotta have this one, be sure to buy it on-sale, and be sure to play it with a game controller.

Okay so here's there's two inherent problems in Batman: Arkham City.

It's a fine game. It's fine. It's not great. It's not the worst. It's a 6/10 if I've ever saw one.

Problem #1: The level designers didn't want to be designing levels for a Batman game. I get it, Batman's got a grappling hook and he can get to a lot of places so it's annoying to have to take all those places into account. But that's the game you chose to make, you know? They just vomit barbed wire along every surface they don't want you to get to, and you just have to accept it like, oh man, it's a shame that Batman doesn't have, like, a tool that can reach out and grab that barbed wire and rip it off of that surface so he can get up there. Like the one he uses to pull items closer to himself. I get it - with certain games you just have to accept the limitations the game devs put upon the player to make it easier on the devs. But it is lazy, and it is absolutely everywhere. And this lazy solution was leaned on so heavily that you can see it manifest even in places without barbed wire. You just can't get up there, because that's not the path the devs designed for you, or that's not the solution for the puzzle they wanted you to have, but they couldn't be bothered to have it make sense for you to not be able to get up there. It's so pervasive that they made it so that Batman has a grappling hook, but you have no direct control over it. It's like a thing that can just happen at some points if you want it to. A prompt appears when it's usable, telling you where it'll pull you to if you do it, but you can't just aim the grappling hook to a platform or surface and have it hook you there, it's only very specific surfaces and platforms that you don't know for sure if it'll work on until you get within range and the prompt appears.

It's like the devs were like "We could make a pretty decent game with the player grappling onto places, and we could make it so the grapple only hooks onto certain materials. The game's world would have to be pretty small, though, so we could design each interactive material to have purpose and to make sense when they can and can't grapple to it."

And the publishers were like, "Nah, it's gonna be a huge open-world, and the main character is Batman. So, y'know. Fuck what you heard."

So they had to make an open-world superhero game against their will while still utilizing the plans they had for a concept that made sense with these mechanics.

Problem #2: Partially due to problem #1, I'm sure, but a lot of the time it feels like I'm arguing with the game as to whether or not I'm allowed to have fun at certain points. I'm constantly being stopped from interacting with things - "Oh, you haven't unlocked the mechanic to get this collectible item yet," or "You haven't unlocked the item required to complete this puzzle yet," and you won't know if it's that or if you just haven't figured out the solution properly until you go and look up the solution online. It's like being given a riddle, and after wracking your brain for ten minutes about what the solution could be you find out that you weren't told the whole riddle, and you don't know how long it'll be before you're told the rest of the riddle. You know what that makes people do? Say "Fuck this shit". The whole enjoyment of a puzzle is knowing that you have all the pieces, and the solution is within your grasp if only you can figure out the right things to do. You don't get that enjoyment with literally any of the puzzles in this game, unless you go out of your way to not even try any of them until you beat the game and you're sure you've unlocked all the extraneous mechanics. And the game is counting on you to do that, it gives you the ability to 'tag' the unattainable puzzle rewards on your map so you can come back to it later when you have the stupid mechanism required to solve it. But nobody except the most anal completionists are going to go out of their way to do that! So in effect all you're doing is keeping me from playing this part of the game, forever! For no reason!

And the unlockable mechanics are egregiously stupid, too. At one point you meet up with Robin - he just appears, because he was concerned about your wellbeing, this wasn't planned by either party ahead of time - and Batman tells him to fuck off and says he's fine, then gives him an assignment that gets him to fuck off to somewhere else. Before he leaves, though, he just hands Batman an item. He doesn't say anything about it, no "Hey moron you left this at home," nothing at all, he just hands him a grappling hook and then leaves.

"But wait, doesn't Batman already have a grappling hook? Like, since the beginning of the game?"

Yes! Yes, he very much does. But this specific grappling hook allows him to attach the hook to flat surfaces and cross gaps.

"But wait, shouldn't he have been able to do that with his normal grappling hook? By like, just attaching it to that surface and then pulling himself over there?"

YES. YES, HE VERY MUCH SHOULD'VE BEEN ABLE TO DO THAT ALREADY. There is absolutely no reason for this mechanic to be withheld from the player until this point! It's not a new item that was just invented that Robin went out of his way to give to Batman, Batman just straight-up didn't bring all of his fucking toys when he started this adventure!

"Well, I mean, was there a reason that Batman may have been underequipped for the situation? Like, was he caught off-guard and without all his tools at the beginning?"

YES! YES, HE VERY MUCH WAS! And they could've used that as a great excuse as to why he would then have to go around fashioning all his standard equipment from shit he found inside the prison, except the game IMMEDIATELY destroys this excuse when Batman shows that he's capable of communicating with Alfred and having him send a goddamned dropship full of his shit inside of it INSIDE THE PRISON AREA. It's got his bat-suit, it's got his basic grappling hook, it's got explosive spray, it's got a whole fuckton of neat gadgets that Batman would obviously have in a situation where he had everything he could want.

AND IT DIDN'T COME WITH THIS OTHER GRAPPLING HOOK THAT DID THIS BASIC-ASSED SHIT A REGULAR GRAPPLING HOOK SHOULD'VE BEEN ABLE TO DO.

Because in this game, the devs love to smack the player's hands off the controller and yell, "NO! You don't get to have fun like that yet! You have to wait! Otherwise we wouldn't know what to give you later to keep the game interesting!"

Which is a piss-poor excuse! It's like if, for the first hour of the game, they made it so you couldn't jump, and then gave you the ability to fucking jump like it was some big fucking deal for you to now be able to do that and not at all a dick move to keep it from you for no reason. And in this hypothetical situation, much like in the real game, they wouldn't have even bothered to give an in-universe reason for you not being able to do this yet. You would just hit the 'jump' button and nothing would happen. No explanation. You would pass by countless places where you'd be like "Man I really wish I could fucking jump, then I could get there." and then suddenly the game does the Zelda-found-an-item jingle and now your goddamned jump button works, whoop-dee-fuckin'-doo. Except now it's been so long that you can't be bothered to retrack all of your steps since the beginning of the game just to check the bits you could've gotten to with a jump button, so really those places might as well not have ever been created.

But first, let's say something good about it. It's chock-full of Riddler puzzles and many of them are clever and fun, and even reaching them can be a puzzle. There are also just far, far too many of them. Getting 100% will be a chore.

OK, on to what's [I]really[/I] bad about this game.

Far too many essential mechanics are either poorly explained in a small note hidden deep in the menus or never explained at all. Too many times I had to look up solutions on the web only to discover that the game never taught me that I could do something very basic. Like being able to glide off walls, or that run-and-skid can go for a long time indeed, or that letting go of the glide button will automatically level you, or that flying into a wall will break it, etc. There are countless examples. And these trick moves are entirely unexpected if you consider that Batman can't do many rudimentary things. Like, jump. That's right! You can swing between buildings like a neurotic Spider-Man but can't jump. Except if you're in combat, in which case you can jump over people. It's as if the game tries to be as counterintuitive as possible.

Controls are generally abysmal. Traversing the open world is a sequence of halting moves and clumsy maneuvering around obstacles and generally feels like shaving with a butter knife. Your grapnel has a mind of its own and often it wants to take you to a building a few blocks away from where you want to go. Things are equally bad in combat, which is surprisingly even worse than in [I]Arkham Asylum[/I]. The only fighting I enjoyed was stealth, which allowed for some basic tactics rather than just the boring mashing of buttons.

Really, this game is a step down from [I]Arkham Asylum[/I] in many ways. Even the presentation is worse! Though the visual engine is more expressive, the designers made some poor choices. The city is washed out in an extremely low-contrast palette so details get lost unless you're standing right in front of them. This is "complemented" by a lot of decidedly clownish bright light points that distract from the little substance that's there. And with some notable exceptions the voice acting is dull, dull, dull. It feels like there's one actor doing the voices of all the NPCs, and it's always a tired wise guy cliché.

[I]Arkham Asylum[/I] did not have an open world but it had big, complex interiors that were a joy to explore. Most buildings here are just a few rooms. And there's a load screen every time you move from the city to the building and back, which utterly breaks immersion.

As for the story, well, true to the open world formula there are a series of plots happening in parallel. This ends up making none of them feel urgent or important and indeed they do not cohere to a single narrative thread. The writing is generally sub par.

I find it incredible that [I]Arkham City[/I] gets so many rave reviews. All in all it's a frustrating and mediocre game. The puzzles are fun, but as a whole I cannot recommend it.

[h2]Full Game Review[/h2]
This is a hard game for me to review. Objectively, Arkham City is a good game. However, I was very disappointed by this game. Maybe it is a product of its time, or maybe my expectations were too high after playing Arkham Asylum, but Arkham City felt like a disappointing sequel. It does not innovate itself enough to warrant existing as a sequel, both narrative and gameplay wise.

[h3]Narrative[/h3]
The pacing of the story was awful and all over the place. They jammed so many villains in the main story, and this left no room for Titan-stuff/Protocol 10 to breath. You were constantly chasing various macguffin for the first half of the game that did nothing to advance the story. Then out of nowhere, the game presents you with a twist regarding Protocol 10. In addition, the twist was so bad that it could have only came from a mustache-twirling villain. To be fair, Arkham Asylum also had a "chase macguffin from villain to villain plot", but that worked as an origin story. If the second entry of your trilogy had no meaningful character nor plot progression, then you are doing something wrong.

It's not all bad though. The second twist regarding Titan-stuff was quite good as it made sense logically/narritively + was foreshadowed. And the boss fight against Mr Freeze's boss fight was was executed (even though it does not make sense narritively for them to fight in the first place, but I digress).

[h3]Gameplay[/h3]
The gameplay felt repetitive due to poor level and quest design. Various locations would get reused throughout the main story mission, which meant navigating through the same corridors multiple times in a single playthrough. And you cannot excuse the game but calling it a metroidvania! Blocking access to parts of the game due to plot-specific reasons should not make it a metroidvania! Walking around in the same crammped cooridors as Batman is the anti-thesis of fun! I would take a thought out, but linear game like Arkham Asylum over something like Arkham City any day. At Asylum had the decency to give previous locations a redesign if they had to be revisited.

Gliding through the city is fun, but gets tedious after a while. There is a huge circular restriction zone right in the middle of the city which cannot be glided through. This forces you to always travel in an arc around the circle, making the city essentially feel like a straight line. And the main quest would often take you go from one end to another which added to the tedium.

On the plus side, Arkham City does include a new gadget that was incorporated in both traversal and combat in an interesting way.

[h3]Conclusion[/h3]
I was initially going to give this game a thumbsup, but then I played Arkham Knight. Now Arkham Knight is not perfect. However, it addressed all issues I had with Arkham City game which makes Arkham City game is easily skippable. And life is too short to play skippable games.

This game is a poorly executed mess that leaves nothing but frustration.

1. Hitboxes:
The hitboxes of the main character are clearly larger than the character model. This is evident when dodging knife attacks or punches from enemies. Even when they visibly miss and hit the air, damage is still applied to the player. This is unacceptable and ruins the combat experience.  

2. Finisher Animations:
The finishing move animations are deliberately slow, allowing enemies to close the distance and attack during the sequence. This feels intentional and makes combat frustrating, especially since these slow animations make it impossible to react in time.  

3. Combos and Controls: 
Some combos work only intermittently, and the game often fails to register key inputs properly. The control system feels clunky and unresponsive, significantly affecting the flow of gameplay.  

4. Harley Quinn's Revenge DLC:
The DLC is riddled with poorly implemented scripts. Enemies deal excessive damage to your armor, far more than in the main game. Sniper and gun-wielding enemies seem overpowered, with much higher health compared to their counterparts in the base game. Even weaker characters like Robin struggle to take down enemies who, logically, should fall after just a few hits.  

5. Electro-Baton NPCs:
The design of enemies with electric batons is nonsensical. Even when you strike them in a way that should disarm them, they somehow manage to deal damage instead. The idea of needing to flank these enemies for a takedown is absurd and unnecessary.  

6. Weapon Retention: 
Enemies holding guns or batons never drop their weapons, no matter how hard you hit them. This completely breaks immersion, as weapons should logically be dropped after a significant hit or during a takedown animation.  

7. General Gameplay:
The overall controls are poorly optimized. Combat and movement feel unpolished, leading to a frustrating and unsatisfying experience.  

Conclusion:
Batman: Arkham City is a disaster in terms of gameplay mechanics and design choices. From broken hitboxes to nonsensical combat mechanics, this game fails on every level. It’s hard to believe this was the product of a professional development team. Avoid this game at all costs.
