So, [b]Arkham Asylum[/b] turned out to be a [i]huge[/i] success. Everybody loved it. And not even because it was an especially good game. It's just the game was so charming and the presentation was so groundbreaking that it was [i]impossible[/i] not to love it. Naturally, the sequel was inevitable. It was also inevitable for it to go open world. Because seventh generation was the time when pretty much everything started to go open world. I never liked the idea (I mean, I still think that the world needs games without an open world and totally believe in the old school genres), but well, the times change. So... here it is. An open world [b]Batman[/b] game.

And you know what? There's a lot of good here. I mean, I actually enjoyed the open world formula here more than I expected. See, I don't like open world games much. I don't mind them from time to time but somehow they all feel pretty much the same to me. And yet, [b]Rocksteady[/b] actually brought their “[b]Batman[/b] simulator” on the whole new level here. Seeing [b]Bat-Signal[/b] in the sky (the idea to use [b]Bat-Signal[/b] as a marker was absolutely brilliant), solving crimes... it actually works. Well, at least on paper. Because the actual game is... A lot of people consider it to be the best one in the main [b]Arkham[/b] series. I heavily disagree. Here's why.

See, it was [b]Rocksteady[/b] first attempt to deal with an open world. Sure, [b]Arkham Asylum[/b] also had that open world[i]ish[/i] feeling, but all in all, it was [b]The Legend of Zelda[/b] clone. Here it's like the real deal. And it's hard not to notice just how much the original formula falls apart. [b]Arkham City[/b] sure had a lot of cons, but it felt whole. In [b]Arkham City[/b] it's like they've added a lot of space between the events and... failed to fill it with stuff. Sure, the core mechanics is still great, but very soon you'll find yourself wanting to skip all those repetitive and meaningless travels. And with no fast travel feature? [i]Yea-a-ah...[/i] Let's just say it's not that exciting.

Sure, some juicy optional quests will help. A lot. Stopping the robberies, hunting down the wanted criminals, dealing with some supervillains... Guess what? There's nothing like that in this game. Well, supervillains [i]are[/i] here, but... those are probably the worst side missions I've ever seen up to this day. Because you know what? Those aren't even missions. Most of those are, like, bloody collectibles. You'll look for [b]Titan[/b] contains for [b]Bane[/b], ringing phones for [b]Zsasz[/b], clues that'll lead you to [b]Deadshot[/b] and so on. No proper markers on map or hints, nothing. Just that. You, looking for some boring crap in a somewhat big city. Imagine how “fun” it is. Heck, they even counted some basic training as side missions!

And to make it even worse, there are... actual... collectibles. Which, again, are the worst collectibles I've ever seen. I mean, [i]technically[/i] the idea was fine. [b]Rocksteady[/b] wanted to make the collectibles hunt more exciting, so, they've attached some sort of action puzzle to most of them. Unfortunately, it only made things worse. After solving a couple of such puzzles, you quickly realize that you're wasting you time. As long as you won't use guides, you'll waste countless hours doing some meaningless crap that won't even feel rewarding. [i]Congratulations![/i] You've just wasted another [b]30[/b] minutes of your life! You can have some random unlockable garbage you probably won't even bother seeing. Joy... And guess how many of such things are in this game? [b]282[/b]. With [b]440 Riddler[/b] challenges total. And you'll need to do at least [b]400[/b] to finish with [b]Nigma[/b]. Should I say that it feels awful? Even those who actually enjoyed the game hated this.

And that's it. That's the entire game. You either waste time on traveling from [b]A[/b] to [b]B[/b] or waste time on collectibles. One way or another, [i]you waste your time[/i]. Just because. It's pretty clear that [b]Rocksteady[/b] failed to create an exciting open world environment so, as the result, they've just filled it with... boring collectibles. The worst thing, though, is the fact that even the presentation suffers from all that. The original movie-like formula doesn't work nearly as good in the open world environment, while the story... See, what was great about [b]Arkham Asylum[/b] is the fact that you didn't really need to know much about [b]Bats[/b] to fully enjoy the story. Here? Even though the game still comes with quite a lot of info on characters, this time you either know your [b]Batman[/b], or there'll be no impact at all. For example, you can't just give people some text and pretend they'll care about characters like [b]Talia al Ghul[/b]. Even the writing this time feels pretty messy. Quite a lot of random things will happen but... like I already said above, the game doesn't feel whole. Sure, the game has its moments. For example, I totally loved the ending and that certain song during the credits? I actually consider it as one of the best moments in [b]Arkham[/b] series (thanks for that, [b]Mr. Hamill[/b]!). And yet, presentation here is not nearly as polished as it was in [b]Arkham Asylum[/b].

The best thing about this game is, probably, the fact that we can play as some other characters now. Thanks to the [b]DLC[/b] that included in [b]GOTY[/b] edition by default. We'll be able to control [b]Robin[/b], [b]Nightwing[/b] and [b]Catwoman[/b]. Which is kinda cool, but... somehow destroys the movie-like feeling even more. For example, unlike [b]Robin DLC[/b], which is, like, stand-alone story, the one with [b]Catwoman[/b] is heavily integrated into the main story and the game will just switch to her at some points without proper reason. Just like that – [i]BOOM![/i] You're a woman now. A [i]cat[/i] woman that is. So... yeah. Not a fan of the [b]DLC[/b] either.

Finally, you know how it is about [b]PC[/b] ports from seventh generation. They suck. And even though what we have here is far from being the worst example, it still comes with a whole bag of nasty technical issues. First of all – in my case the game refused to work with wireless gamepad. Not the biggest problem in the world and [b]Arkham Asylum[/b] had the same issue, but still, using the wires just to be able to play the certain game? It's annoying. And guess what? There's another gamepad-related issue. The one that can actually break all the achievements. No idea how it works, but the fact stays – there's a gamepad-related issue that can block all the achievements. Also, the game is terribly optimized (not nearly as badly as those early versions of [b]Arkham Knight[/b], of course, but still), it'll crash from time and so on. Ridiculously long loading times from the [b]SSD[/b] included. As the result, even though I kinda liked how the game looks in [b]4K[/b], I actually felt like I miss the times when I played it on my good ol' [b]Xbox 360[/b]. So glad we rarely get such poor ports nowadays...

One way or another, I totally consider [b]Arkham City[/b] to be the worst game in the main series. It was, like, a bold  attempt to create complicated open world experience with [b]Batman[/b]. But while breaking the original [b]Arkham Asylum[/b] formula in order to achieve something bigger, [b]Rocksteady[/b] was unable to achieve the same level of success that we'll see in [b]Arkham Knight[/b]. It's just that. [b]Arkham City[/b] is a transferring point between the [b]Asylum[/b] and the [b]Knight[/b]. Not an [b]Asylum[/b] already, but not yet the [b]Knight[/b]. When I think about the [b]Asylum[/b], I think about very solid movie-like presentation. But when I think 'bout this game? All I think about are empty world and tons of annoying collectibles. Sure, quite a lot of the original charm is still here and so are everybody's favorite voice actors, but...............

Batman: Arkham City is a gorgeous game. It features some of the best voice acting in any medium and very probably the best actor to have ever played Batman. The setting is very Burton-esque in a good way (unlike the Burton films) and is very large and filled with things to do....

Sort of. For a sandbox, I can't find a single thing I can decide to do any differently than the preordained method. You might assume that gadget use during combat is an example of decision making, but it leads to the same result as starting a conventional brawl or sneaking around (minus the sneaking experience point bonus). You can do the Riddler challenges the way the Riddler has decreed (or rather, the developers by proxy) or you can fail. Same with brawling, same with stealth, same with proper gadget use. Everything in this game is coreographed. You can get around Arkham City fairly quickly to "explore", but the only real differences between any two areas are cosmetic. And a great majority of the places you might find interesting are walled off until you've successfully jumped through whichever hoops are required to access them. And by then, the sense of novelty grows very bitter. In all my time spent with this game I couldn't find a single genuinely interactive, malleable, thing. Even breaking into the villain's strongholds is done according to the path the developers have laid out for you.

So overall, it's got excellent writing and acting in a beautiful setting, but it's not a sandbox game. More like an obedience course for humans. You can do things the "right" way, and in the "right" order, or you fail. That applies to every aspect of Arkham City. And yes, the same thing can be said of Mega Man 2 (for example), and it's still a classic, but it's not a sandbox. There's no presumption of an open world or freedom of choice in Mega Man 2, but there certainly is in Arkham City. And that's why it gets the thumbs down. Mechanically it's a Telltale game being passed off as an open world game. Even the combat is made of a series of quicktime events masquerading as attacks and dodges. And before you go around assuming that this game will put you in Batman's shoes (so to speak), by all means look up a video online of the Detective Mode being used to investigate a crime scene. There are several of those sequences in Arkham City, but what they boil down to is "find the thing you're supposed to, using the vision mode you're supposed to, while waiting for the occasional dialogue prompt". Something tells me Batman would never have to wait around impatiently for the grown-ups to finish talking... to solve a murder.

I'm going to review each separate part of the game

I recommend playing the main story and the non-tedious side missions only if you do buy this game. The whole package I don't recommend in general though because the other parts of the game aren't that great. Especially the boring-as-hell challenges.

Main Story

I hate the combat in these games with a passion. Mainly because your character's movements are mostly arbitrary and you have no idea what exactly they will do other than "attack" or "counter". You don't know which direction they will counter in, which enemy they will target next, you have little agency in movement during combat. Battles last forever. It feels like crap. It's easy too, but when you "lose" ever it's because of the above issues, not because you made some sort of mistake. After all, all you have to do is press A to attack and Y occasionally when you need to counter. Whether the game allows those attacks to connect with an optimal enemy or one with 50 other enemies around them is up to the game though. You have other techniques you can do, but no real way of indicating which enemy to do any of them on for sure, so it feels like you just hope the game does it on the right enemy for all your attacks and actions. Enemy about to shoot you? Sorry you targeted a different enemy and got shot and died. You couldn't do anything about it - it's just the game's decision. WHY CAN'T I HIT MULTIPLE ENEMIES AT ONCE WITH SWEEPING KICKS OR SOMETHING IF THEY SURROUND ME? You have no agency in combat other than punch one guy, counter the guy who ran up behind you - maybe use a gadget and hope it targets the right enemy. Dealing with multiple enemies at once is out of the question outside of some special attacks you can occasionally use that stun them, you can never kill multiple enemies in one go, that'd be a fun and quicker. You have to suffer through punching each enemy one-by-one to kill them. Or spend 200 years creeping up on each enemy like it's dishonored (much better game) if the room layout lets you.

The graphics are great. The story is quite interesting, and the exploration of the city and light puzzle solving elements are fun. This game isn't all that long so the reliance on "bat-vision" isn't too annoying. I actively just avoid combat since it's such a drag. At least the game gives you options to take out opponents without having to start another brainless boring brawl session. Great voice acting and the appearance of each superhero/supervillain look fairly accurate to their original designs. I appreciate that aspect. I'm not much of a superhero fan but it was interesting seeing all these supervillains in the game.

There are simply too many riddler collectibles. I got all of them, but it gets to be a drag after a while. Rather than pepper the world with things that give you a tiny amount of EXP that look exactly the same, pepper the world with actual interesting experiences and encounters. Focus on side missions with actual interactions with characters, and if you need collectibles, have a smaller amount that give you something particularly useful like a new optional gadget or skill or something.

Challenge pack DLC / Riddler's Revenge

Absolutely abysmal DLC / extra content that is just "fight some enemies" times one million. The combat in these games is the most boring part. The exploration is more interesting and the light puzzle solving as well. No I don't care about getting a combo of two million (mashing A and Y and maybe B for fun) for three hours to get a medal and an achievement. F*** off with this garbage. I'm glad this fad of "attack and wait to counter and no enemy lock-on" went out of style eventually. Arkham Asylum, Shadow of Mordor, and this game are the ones with that combat style I've played and I'm already completely sick of it. There's a reason the achievement rates for this part of the game are the lowest out of the whole package. It's not fun and takes forever.

Harley Quinn's revenge

It's a small DLC that focuses on story and combat. It's essentially another mission that adds on to the main story, and is pretty good just like the rest of the main game but honestly if I bought this dlc separately I would feel like it isn't worth whatever you could charge because it's such a small thing and is almost completely reuse of assets in the steel mill area of the main game's map. Nothing much to it, and almost entirely just fighting trash normal enemies too.

Overall this whole Arkham City game would have been recommendable if it wasn't padded with so many awful combat sessions. If you play the game just for the story it's more fun than trying to do the soul-sucking challenges. So I'd recommend if you just play the story, but don't recommend the other parts.

There's one important caveat I need to mention since nobody ever criticizes this game's combat, and judging from the forums, blindly defend this game no matter what. Spamming the counter attack button can wipe out a crowd of seven guys without suffering any damage to yourself. You don't even have to face them to counter, rendering the first few hours a complete joke. 

The worst part of the game is that the melee combat system also has an annoying auto-targeting system which means you aren't guaranteed to hit the person you're aiming at. Of all the games that copied this fighting system, THEY ALL DID IT BETTER. Button prompts in the middle of fight just gets old after a couple hours. This game has a lot going for it. Up until the final act it's an incredibly enjoyable well-paced experience. The amount of Batman villains you interact with is impressive in itself. The penguin, Mr.Freeze, Two-Face, the Joker, Harley Quinn, Hugo Strange, Ras al Ghul, The Mad Hatter, Deadshot, The Riddler, Bane, Zsasz, Solomon Grundy, Calendar Man, Clayface. Looking at that sheer amount of villains, all more or less in great form, it's downright impressive the scope of the game. However, as you go on the game starts to show its cracks. 


You tie things up very hastily and with a weird end with Mr.Freeze and the third act begins. Suddenly a well paced story throws all the plot points out the window and you have no new interactions with main villains just sitting in buildings across the map. The mastermind Strange's plan to threaten Batman and take over from the inside and coordinate such an amazing end is here... and his plan is to drop bombs on convicts. That's seriously it. That's protocol 10, that's the entire buildup. Entire story threads are abandoned, Jokers blood in hospitals, Strange knowing Bruce's identity, why Titan is even in this game, why Harley is even in this game, the gang war between Two-Face, Penguin and the Joker. All of these are just left hanging, making you wonder why they were even introduced. 



Now you're at "The AAA End" fighting Hugo Strange, you punch him once and he's beaten, then Ras al Ghul comes in and immediately kills Strange and then dies as an immortal person, then Talia dies by Joker. Two seconds later Joker is clayface and then you kill Clayface and then next second Joker dies, and with his dead love on the ground Batman carries out Jokers body, never saying a single word about any of the events of the last 3 hours. The entire end sequence is probably about 5 minutes total in runtime. No comments about any of the events at the end of the game. Then the game ends, cut to black screen. Really? That's what everything was leading up to. 

Oh, but you have the GOTY edition so you're immediately Catwoman fighting Two-Face in maybe the worst section in the game which cannot end fast enough with 2 words spoken by Two-Face. Now you're Batman again and you're back in the city for some reason still without ANY comment on the events of the game resolving (not really). It's very hard to see why anyone would find satisfaction out of beating this game


There's a LOT to love in City, but all that love, provided you're doing the side content as it comes up instead of the main story first, is all in the first 2/3 of the game. Almost none of that is waiting for you in the ending act. The last act of the game is so rushed and breakneck-paced and wraps up with such a sloppy and fast resolution it makes the rest of the game look bad. I'd be surprised, if I counted, if they spent more than 20 seconds on the Joker dying, I'd be even more surprised if they spent more than ACTUALLY 3 seconds on Batman having the love of his life die in front of him. There's not a single line about any of this, there's nothing in the main game saying or acknowledging or commenting on any of the entire back end of the game where it does so for the rest. 


It really seems like they got to the end of the game and had to slap it together, it's so bad at the end that I got whiplash hearing about the spotless record this game holds with people with how poor and completely half-baked the entire ending of this game is and how all the care given  to the world in City before the ending is completely gone. Despite the bombings, and Joker's death and Strange's death and Ras Al Ghul and Talia Al Ghul's death and Protocol 10 and the city in ruins none of the villains care in their respective places, there are no new developments. Instead they all leave off at this weird intersection where you lock most of them away and they have nothing else to say. It feels so hollow, where the game is leading in the middle act to the beginning of the end is so interesting and they throw all that out at the end. 


And the women in this game, I cannot believe I hadn't heard someone mention it before. Every. Single. Woman has maxed out sliders, every single woman is overtly sexualised even if they don't get a name. Harley Quinn is a damsel, Catwoman a few times is a damsel, Talia is a damsel. The amount of times the word 'bitch' is thrown out in the few times women are centered in this story is pretty shocking. Really am wondering what Rocksteady was doing reducing some of the most iconic women characters to footnotes to objectify and put in the background, only pulling them forward to call them a bitch. I mean hell, Bruce is literally trying to let THOUSANDS DIE because he loves Talia so much and yet she dies practically off-screen, she is killed and they spend maybe 2 seconds and a short quip about it. The game also ignores that you leave her body and walk out with the Joker's over hers. WHAT was Rocksteady thinking with that end. 


You have all these pieces, you have all these thematic ties and interesting ways you can tell the devs read the comics and had all the little details in the world and yet it says nothing with the themes. It does nothing with them, there is 0 exploration of any of the central themes of batman in an entire story about Batman. The writing is so shoddy the further you go, and Bruce is actually just a brick. There's nothing you're going to get, you're lucky to get a single line unless it's about the Joker. 


Poison Ivy is in the game, has her own whole section of the map but Batman can't even get in. Killer Croc is in the game but you speak to him once if you know where to find the secret area. 


All the characters that are given mainline-level attention like Freeze and the Penguin are abandoned and left in weird states by the time you go to beat the game. It feels like so much of the game is SUPPOSED to wrap up but does not. The wrap up you do get is so sloppy it's hard to see what Rocksteady was even trying to do here. It's not super surprising, Asylum's end is universally derided for being a mess, I'm just very confused to not hear the same consensus on the slapped-together ending for this game too. They just can't seem to figure out how to end a game. They know how to set it up and dig deep and go into such detail you'll probably never even notice but when it comes to big storyline resolution they throw their hands up. The ending has less attention paid to it than the side missions, it's so disappointing



Honestly, having a perspective on this game now, separate from the hype and over-praise of this game at the time, I'd recommend stopping before re-entering the steel mill for the last time. I felt the last act was so jarring in its rushed and flimsy storytelling and gameplay that you'd be much more likely to love this game having stopped before the end begins. It's kind of insane to hear 0 criticisms of this game with an entire ending act like THAT. If this is what is hailed as a "perfect" video game story the medium has a LONG way to go. This would be endlessly ridiculed online if not in the form of the game, I cannot stress how sloppy the ending is. Up until that point though? Fantastic game, it's probably an 8.5 before you re-enter the Steel Mill for the final time. By the time I finished and beat that Two-Face boss? It's sitting at about a 6. Game is a mess the second you try and beat it, really leaves a sour taste after such amazing setup. I'd really love to recommend this game, but on sheer principle I cannot.

[h1]READ THIS BEFORE LAUNCHING THE GAME[/h1]

During the installation process, along with the DirectX libraries another program will be installed called [b]AMD Dual-Core Optimizer[/b], which was meant to improve the performance on systems that run Windows XP and use old AMD Dual-Core CPUs.

On PCs that run Windows Vista and later and/or an Intel CPU, you won't need that program because it will impact the performance and cause other issues.

Unfortunately when you launch the game for the first time you don't get the choice to decline the installation of AMD Dual-Core Optimizer (that's why I left a negative review).
In order to stop that program from being installed, do as follows:

[i]If the program is already installed, you should uninstall it. Go to "Programs and Features", select "AMD Dual-Core Optimizer" and click "Uninstall" (perhaps it's going to take a while, do not cancel the process and wait for it to finish); afterwords, reboot the PC.[/i]

    1) Go to the installation folder of the game (right click on the game title -> properties -> local files tab -> browse local files)
    2) Open "installscript.vdf" (right click -> open with -> use Notepad)
    3) Scroll down until you see the word "AMD", followed by a bunch of code between the two perpendicular { and } brackets; delete that portion of code, beginning from the word "AMD" to the last perpendicular bracket (note that you must leave the brackets on the left side and everything else)
    4) Save the file. Make sure you didn't delete anything that has to do with DXSetup, VCRedist_x86 and DotNetFx35
    5) When you're done, go to the "Setup" folder and delete "amd_dc_opt.exe" (this is an optional step, just to be safe)

If you've done everything correctly, when you launch the game the installation of AMD Dual-Core Optimizer won't start.

[b]REMEMBER TO NOT VERIFY THE INTEGRITY OF GAME FILES, OTHERWISE YOU MUST REPEAT THE ENTIRE PROCEDURE.[/b]

It's tough to give this a binary "Recommended / Not Recommended" review here, but ultimately I think I have to give it a Thumbs Down. The continuation from Asylum was great. I enjoy the combat, even if some of the later brawls were just a ridiculous amount of enemies in single rooms. The rooms where you sneakily take down sentries one-by-one is fun, even if they copy/paste that formula repeatedly in the same rooms. The story is exactly what I would expect from a Batman game, and I enjoyed the inclusion of classic Batman characters throughout. I really liked the idea of the open-world map, and while I think Asylum's smaller map led to tighter segments, expanding that to a full "city" was a cool to see.

That being said, I think the city kinda collapsed under it's own weight. Movement was incredibly unfun. In a post-Insomnia Spider-Man world, it wasn't nearly as zippy enough, nor was it particularly dangerous to move between regions. It just felt like a slog. This was made worse by there being a large impenetrable wall in the middle of map, forcing you to go the long way around constantly throughout the game. It didn't take long to make this feel like a chore instead of an engaging part of the gameplay. It obviously wanted you to interact with the collectibles along the way, like the Riddler trophies, but so many of those require gadgets you get later, it feels bad to try and remember ALL of them to return to later. Once I decided I wasn't going to get them all, I didn't care to stop and explore the map.

This really was just made worse by the Catwoman DLC. Since I'm playing the GOTY version a decade after release, I didn't realize this was bonus content and just played her segments as part of the base experience. She shows up so infrequently, and her segments are so underbaked, it ultimately felt really bad to play her (especially since she had practically no upgrades by the end).

While I did find the story serviceable, I did think the ending was very underwhelming, especially since it cuts right to a Catwoman segment. I felt like I was missing a good ending or something due to how abruptly things resolve. I guess they're hinting at the third game in the trilogy, but it still felt like it's missing something.

I think at this point, you've made your mind up on whether you're playing this decade-old game in a lauded trilogy. It's definitely worth a shot if you want to experience the Arkham games. But I couldn't really see myself returning to this in the same way I might revisit Asylum in the future. Just too much busywork and not enough pay-off.

Batman: Arkham City is a really underwhelming game. It honestly doesn’t succeed in any facet. Its gameplay is unengaging. Its story is abysmal. Its characters are uncompelling. It is needlessly padded out with tons of filler. It’s dragged down by a host of issues. The game does not deserve “Overwhelmingly positive” reviews. I can only imagine it received such widespread adulation because it is a Batman game and it certainly is a Batman game, but is it good? No. Is it terrible? No. It’s middling at best.

The combat is unsatisfying. It can be fun here and there, but there just isn’t any depth. It doesn’t feel earned. I didn’t come away from it feeling like Batman. I felt like I was just playing a very violent rhythm game. On top of that, it’s weird in practice, too. Sometimes Batman will leap across two screens to attack a bad guy, then he’ll fumble an attack on a bad guy right next to him. There’s no rhyme or logic to it. And you’ll be pissed off when it happens because you then lose your combo for no good reason.

The game is utterly filled with content, but that doesn’t mean it is good content. It is Filler City. It is seriously padded out with a lot of meaningless content that is either trifling at best or just atrocious at worst. It suffers all the pitfalls of a Ubisoft-style open-world and is no more compelling for it. The side activities are shoddily implemented and feel tacked on as a way to expose the player to more of Batman’s rogues gallery. Unfortunately, it just doesn’t work for creating a fun or interesting experience. Why would I care to see more of these characters when the experience is the same for every one of them? They aren’t interesting to see. They are window dressing. I feel like 75-85% of the game could have easily been cut. And the resources dedicated to more meaningful, interesting content. 


The story is just abysmal. Batman himself is completely uninteresting here and the central dilemma plaguing him and the world at large is equally uncompelling. He has zero personality beyond delivering gruff lines to everyone around him while all the characters you interact with are homicidal maniacs that would be better off dead. The villains are particularly heinous here and it beggars belief that Batman lets them live after the crap they pull off repeatedly in the game. Even the villains that aren’t wholly evil act idiotic here, too, and it drags the story down even further.

There are two massive drivers of events in the game and one is completely shrouded in mystery til the very end, so you have zero reason to care about it. And the other is much more immediate, but due to the flat performances and needlessly tacked on filler, it doesn’t feel urgent at all. It is barely a blip in your mind. And you feel there are no stakes whatsoever to what you are doing.

I know Batman is a gruff character with a somber demeanor, but he’s more than that. We have seen him across a large variety of media. And he can be so much more. And be more dynamic and interesting. He’s complex with a lot of issues that extend well beyond the surface. And we just don’t see any of that here. It’s just the most surface-level interpretation of Batman being Batman and that’s that. 

I came away from this game feeling like I may have enjoyed parts of it, but it was ultimately just a tedious experience and after playing other games, my opinion has been revised downwards. It just isn’t a good game. It wasn’t even a good game for its time. I’ve played a ton of games from its time period recently and it doesn’t measure up to any of them. I know my opinion is in the minority, but hey, it is what it is.

Sorry to say, but this game is inferior to [i]Arkham Asylum[/i] in my opinion, adding unnecessary complexity to an already-established design. There's not much positive I can say here, honestly.

The major element of [i]Arkham Asylum[/i] that I enjoyed was the confined metroidvania layout of its map, giving a tighter focus on the cast of characters (which was nice for me, as a newcomer to the DC Universe). Sure, [i]Arkham City[/i]'s evolution to a less claustrophobic, more linear and open layout is impressive for its generation, paving the way for future games like Insomniac's [i]Spider-Man[/i], it's still primitive in its design, lacking choices existing in games prior to it, notably fast travel.
And don't even get me started on this combat. I'm in full agreement that [i]Arkham Asylum[/i]'s brawling did feel a bit barebones. However, in building upon these systems through more moves and weapons, it not only adds complexity to controls and systems as a whole, but it often feels broken when trying to land hits. There would be several occasions where I would try to pull a knockout move on an enemy, only for it to be canceling out because the animation didn't finish before I get hit by an attack I couldn't even counter, leading me to question whether or not I was going to have to just mash buttons for 5 minutes straight. In certain moments, it's frustrating (especially when the final boss is way easier than the encounters prior).

I found the narrative to be weaker this time around too, putting partial blame on its more open nature. It's much more simple, seemingly focusing on Batman and Joker's own mortalities than a major threat itself, culminating into one of the most anti-climactic endings I've ever experienced in a video game story. Doctor Hugo Strange is a character I was very much intrigued by, given his mysterious and menacing nature. But by the time I reached the final act, learning about his true motive and still not fully understanding what the hell "Protocol 10" even is, it felt all for nothing. What's even more crazy is that, having played the latest version of this game, I didn't realize until afterwards that these Catwoman interludes are just DLC and not part of the original game, which makes it even more disappointing that it wasn't a launch choice to begin with, given the added nature to her relationship with Batman during the narrative.

[i]Batman: Arkham City[/i] overextends itself as a sequel to what came before it, sacrificing a tight narrative and design with something more technically impressive than anything during the generation. It's not a bad game and it has some moments of stealth and action that shine through, but it's definitely one that I'll probably never understand its full praise for, other than maybe how abrupt its final act is. If you want me to invest in this world and cast of characters, don't make the world so vast and fluffed... or let me at least land a hit without wanting to throw my controller down.

Despite the combat being significantly better, I found the story in Arkham City less interesting than its predecessor's, especially since it kept bringing in characters halfway through storylines that it refuses to introduce or elaborate on. Because of that, for instance, I had no investment in Talia, or, in another case, I would have no idea who Clayface and Grundy were if I hadn't played f****** LEGO Batman. Not everything is bad here, I liked the side mission design, but even that positive comes with the asterisk of this game's Riddles, which are truly horrendous due to an overabundance of them (440!) and often having really annoying or confusing solutions. I personally wouldn't recommend this game, and I hate to say that because I typically adore Batman media, but I really didn't like this game's story, and the side content and most other parts of the gameplay weren't good enough to make up for that.
